body:
The Edison literature sweep surfaced two records whose reports identify a
confident ontology term while explicitly refusing to assert an identity mapping:

| record | term | report's words |
|---|---|---|
| `Calf brains` | `UBERON:0000955` *brain* | "high-confidence anatomical-source annotation" but "do **not** assert `skos:exactMatch` or `skos:closeMatch`" |
| `Cow manure` | `ENVO:00003031` *animal manure* | recommends retaining UNMAPPED |

Both terms resolve correctly against the local builds, and both prefixes are
already in `promote_resolved_unmapped.py`'s `ONTOLOGY_DB`.

The reports forbid `exactMatch` and `closeMatch` — the two predicates that
license node substitution. They do not mention `skos:narrowMatch`, which is
exactly the predicate that says the subject is *narrower than* the object
without claiming they are interchangeable, and which MAPPING_SEMANTICS.md
Section 3 already uses for hydrates (`NaH2PO4*H2O` narrowMatch the anhydrous
`CHEBI:37585`).

So the question is a policy one, not a lookup one: **is Section 3's
identifier + narrowMatch + Rule B1 registry row pattern meant only for
hydrate/salt variants of a parent compound, or does it also cover
source-qualified materials** — calf brains as a narrower thing than brain, cow
manure than animal manure, larchwood xylan than xylan?

Arguments each way:

- **For extending it.** These records would gain a real, correct, non-substituting
  edge into UBERON/ENVO, which is more than the current UNMAPPED conveys. The
  narrowMatch semantics are literally true.
- **Against.** "Calf brains" as a medium ingredient is a *preparation*, and
  narrowMatch on a preparation-to-anatomy axis is a different relation from
  narrowMatch on a hydrate-to-anhydrous axis. Conflating them makes the
  predicate mean two things, and kg-microbe consumers cannot tell which.
  UBERON:0000955 as an *anatomical source* — which is what the report actually
  recommends — is arguably a schema slot, not an SSSOM row.

Nothing was applied; the records stay UNMAPPED and the CURIEs are recorded in
their curation history. Raising this because the same question governs a
recurring class of records (extracts, tissue preparations, source-qualified
polymers), and deciding it once is better than deciding it per record.

Blocked on a curator's call; see also #236 on subject/file identity.
title: Does the Section 3 narrowMatch pattern extend to source-material records?

body:
Hit twice now, in #114 and again applying Edison research.

`scripts/merge_unmapped_into_mapped.py` folds an UNMAPPED record into a MAPPED one as a `RAW_TEXT` synonym. It refuses when the source carries anything a synonym cannot represent:

```
'Na2Glycerophosphate.5H2O': source carries data a synonym cannot represent
  (ingredient_type, occurrence_statistics(1/1), synonyms(1 beyond the self-reference));
  merge it by hand or extend this script
```

The refusal is **right in principle** — silently dropping occurrences or an `ingredient_type` would lose real data, and it is what caught the `MES buffer` (`STOCK_SOLUTION`) vs `MES` (`SINGLE_INGREDIENT`) distinction in #114, which was a genuine semantic difference worth stopping for.

But it now blocks the ordinary case too. Two spelling variants of one substance —

```
Na2glycerophosphate•5H2O    (grounded to cas:13408-09-8 from Edison research)
Na2Glycerophosphate.5H2O    punctuation variant
Na2Glycerophosphate•5H2O    capitalisation variant
```

— cannot be merged, because each carries `occurrence_statistics(1/1)` and an `ingredient_type`. Those are exactly the fields `merge_mapped_records.py` already knows how to transfer: it **sums** occurrences and unions role facets, and #196 taught it to carry `source_occurrences` per source as well.

So the capability exists; it just lives in the wrong script. The asymmetry is:

| | occurrences | ingredient_type | source_id |
|---|---|---|---|
| `merge_mapped_records` | summed | — | carried to history |
| `merge_unmapped_into_mapped` | **refuses** | **refuses** | carried to history |

Suggested: reuse `merge_mapped_records.transfer_occurrences()` (extracted in #196 precisely so it could be shared) and allow the merge when the source and target `ingredient_type` **agree** — keeping the refusal only when they differ, which is the `MES buffer` case the check exists for.

Until then, variant-label cleanup on unmapped records needs a hand-edit, which is what #267 was filed about.

Related: #114, #196, #267, #218.
title: merge_unmapped_into_mapped refuses any source carrying occurrences or ingredient_type — the common case

body:
Found reviewing PR #266 (#263).

All four records re-grounded in #263 had `molecular_formula` / `inchi` / `smiles` (and one `pubchem_cid`) written onto them by `AUTO_BACKFILL_CHEBI_CHEMISTRY`, copied from the CHEBI term the record pointed at. When that term is wrong, the backfill silently manufactures wrong chemistry that looks curated.

`Casamino acids` shows the worst of it. It is a casein hydrolysate — an undefined mixture — and was correctly typed `UNDEFINED_MIXTURE` by a rule matching the name. Then:

1. The record was grounded to CHEBI:78020 *heptacosanoate* (wrong).
2. `AUTO_BACKFILL_CHEBI_CHEMISTRY` wrote heptacosanoate's `C27H53O2` / InChI / SMILES onto it.
3. `auto_classify_ingredient_type` saw populated chemical structure and **re-typed the record `SINGLE_INGREDIENT`**, overwriting the correct classification — its own history says *"chemical structure populated (molecular_formula)"*.

So one wrong id cascaded into wrong structure and a wrong record type, each step looking like a legitimate automated curation entry in `curation_history`. Nothing flagged the contradiction between `ingredient_type=UNDEFINED_MIXTURE` and "has a single exact molecular formula".

Worth considering:
- **Record provenance on backfilled fields.** If `molecular_formula` carried "derived from `<curie>`", re-grounding could invalidate it automatically instead of relying on a curator to notice. (#138 is the same shape: stale derived columns outranking corrections.)
- **Do not let a derived field drive a classification.** `auto_classify_ingredient_type` promoting `UNDEFINED_MIXTURE` → `SINGLE_INGREDIENT` on the strength of a backfilled formula lets a grounding error rewrite the record's identity.
- **Flag the contradiction.** A name matching a known complex/mixture pattern *and* a single exact formula is a signal worth surfacing.

PR #266 drops the poisoned fields on the four affected records rather than recomputing them, but does not address the mechanism — any future wrong grounding will do this again.

Related: #263, #266, #138, #237.
title: AUTO_BACKFILL_CHEBI_CHEMISTRY propagates a wrong grounding into structure fields and can flip ingredient_type

body:
Found reviewing PR #266 (#263).

The repo has `scripts/reground_mapped_record.py`, whose own help says it *"moves a mapped record to a different term"* and that it **refuses when the destination CURIE is already held**. That refusal is precisely the safety check the #263 work needed.

I re-grounded four records by hand-editing the YAML instead, and duly minted two identifiers that were already held (`CHEBI:66870`, `FOODON:03315719`). `just qc-duplicate-ids` caught it — so the net is fine — but the failure came *after* the edit, the collection re-sync, the product re-export, and the SSSOM reconcile had all been run on bad state, and unwinding that cost more than the edit itself.

Nothing points a curator at the tool at the moment they need it:

- `MAPPING_SEMANTICS.md` describes the mapping *semantics* but names no script for changing an existing grounding.
- The `map-media-ingredients` and `merge-ingredients` skills cover mapping new records and merging, not re-grounding a wrong one.
- `just --list` has no re-ground recipe, so the script is invisible unless you already know it exists (`merge_mapped_records.py` at least gets referenced from the duplicate-gate failure text).

Suggestions, cheapest first:
1. Add the re-ground script to the `qc-duplicate-ids` failure message, next to the existing `--write-baseline` hint — that is exactly where someone who just made this mistake is looking.
2. Add a `just reground` recipe so it appears in `just --list`.
3. Cross-reference it from `MAPPING_SEMANTICS.md` and the `map-media-ingredients` skill.

Related: #263, #266, #224, #218.
title: reground_mapped_record.py exists and refuses collisions — but nothing steers a curator to it

Found reviewing PR #264 (#261).

`mapped_ingredients.csv` is now gated by two targets — `mapped_csv` (canonical label) and `mapped_csv_curator_label` (curator label) — which is intentional: they check different columns with different severities. The side effect is that the **summary totals count every row of that file twice**:

```
OK_ID_ONLY:          2118  ->  4129     (+2011, ~= the file's row count)
SKIPPED_NO_ADAPTER:  3757  ->  3943
```

Nothing is wrong with the findings themselves — the per-finding rows in `reports/label_drift.tsv` carry a `surface` column and are correctly attributed. It is only the aggregate line of `just validate-products` / `just report-label-drift` that now reads as if the corpus grew by ~2000 records.

Low severity, but it makes the summary a poor trend signal: anyone comparing run-to-run totals across this change sees a jump that reflects gating topology, not data.

Options:
- Print the summary broken down per target (most informative, largest change).
- Or emit a one-line note when a glob is gated by more than one target, so the double count is explicit rather than surprising.

Related: #261, #264.
title: The correspondence summary double-counts mapped_ingredients.csv now that two targets gate it

body:
Found in review of #234.

The SSSOM `curie_map` expands `MIM:` to `.../data/ingredients/mapped/`, so `MIM:<slug>` is meant to address the per-record file. But `export_individual_records.FilenameIndex` **deliberately never renames an existing file** — it preserves the original stem so per-record paths stay stable.

So when a record's `preferred_term` changes, the SSSOM subject slug changes and the file stem does not:

    SSSOM subject: MIM:2-phenylethylamine
    file on disk:  data/ingredients/mapped/Phenethylamine_Hydrochloride.yaml

Measured on #234's branch: SSSOM subjects with no matching file stem went **7 → 8** (7 pre-existing, 1 added by that PR's relabel).

Nothing currently checks this. `reconcile_sssom.py` validates GAP/ORPHAN/STALE on `ontology_id` and never looks at the subject slug, which is why #234's "reconcile 0" reassurance did not cover it.

## Options

1. Teach `export_individual_records` to rename when `preferred_term` changes, and accept that per-record paths are not permanently stable.
2. Accept that `MIM:` slugs are opaque identifiers rather than file paths, and say so in the curie_map documentation — then the mismatch is not a defect.
3. Add a check that every `MIM:` subject resolves to a file, and fix the 7 pre-existing cases.

(2) is probably right — stable per-record paths are worth more than slug/path agreement — but it should be a stated decision, since today the curie_map implies (1).

Related: #234, #209.
title: Relabelling a record leaves its MIM: SSSOM subject pointing at a filename that no longer matches

body:
Raised in review of #234 and worth recording rather than waving off.

MIM's record now named `2-phenylethylamine` (CHEBI:18397) carries:

    cas_rn: 64-04-0
    data_source: CultureBotHT compounds_to_cas.csv

`64-04-0` is phenethylamine, the **free base**, and is ChEBI's own xref for CHEBI:18397. But the record's original `preferred_term` was **"Phenethylamine Hydrochloride"**. So CultureBotHT paired a hydrochloride catalogue name with a free-base CAS.

Two readings, and the record cannot distinguish them:

1. **The name was wrong** — the ingredient really is the free base, someone typed a salt name. #234 took this reading and renamed the record, because ChEBI has no phenethylamine hydrochloride term (the only `C8H11N.HCl` is CHEBI:191064, *N*-methylbenzylamine hydrochloride) and every other datum on the record is the free base.
2. **The CAS lookup was wrong** — the ingredient really is the hydrochloride (CAS 156-28-5) and CultureBotHT's name→CAS step dropped the salt. In that case the record should be a hydrate/salt-style grounding, not a rename.

#234 chose (1) and the stakes are low — the record has **0 occurrences**, so no medium depends on it. But the same `compounds_to_cas.csv` source feeds other records, and if its name→CAS step silently drops salt forms then other salt-named records may carry free-base CAS numbers.

## Worth checking

Scan records whose `chemical_properties.data_source` is `CultureBotHT compounds_to_cas.csv` for a `preferred_term` containing a salt/hydrate word (hydrochloride, sulfate, sodium salt, …) whose `cas_rn` resolves to the parent instead. That tells you whether this is one bad row or a systematic step.

Related: #234, #228, #218.
title: CHEBI:18397's cas 64-04-0 came from a salt catalogue name — verify the pairing

body:
Found reviewing #231, which introduces the ambiguity by publishing synonyms.

Before #231, `docs/data/*.csv` carried only `preferred_term`, and **preferred_terms are unique** (verified: zero duplicates). So the CSV supported an unambiguous `{label: identifier}` join. Publishing synonyms makes that join order-dependent for **87 labels**.

The sharp cases are where **one record's `preferred_term` is another record's synonym** — a consumer's answer depends purely on row order:

| label | holders |
|---|---|
| `Vitamin B12` | CHEBI:176843 (preferred) / CHEBI:17439 (synonym) / UNMAPPED_0005 (synonym) |
| `Mannitol` | CHEBI:29864 (preferred) / CHEBI:16899 (synonym) |
| `Tryptophan` | CHEBI:27897 (preferred) / CHEBI:16828 (synonym) |
| `Citrate` | CHEBI:16947 (preferred) / CHEBI:30769 (synonym) |
| `Sulfur` | CHEBI:26833 (preferred) / CHEBI:17909 (synonym) |
| `Putrescine` | CHEBI:17148 (preferred) / cas:333-93-7 (synonym) |

…and ~12 more of that shape.

Some of these are the #218 family in another guise — `Citrate`/`Citric acid`, `Sulfur`, `Mannitol` are the same substance under two CHEBI ids, i.e. the inverse defect of #225. Others are legitimately shared synonyms where two distinct terms both accept a loose common name.

#231 does **not** treat this as a failure — a synonym legitimately can be shared, and failing the build on it would block the fix. The gate prints it as a note.

## What to decide

1. Which of the 87 are the #225/#218 inverse defect (one substance, two ids) and should be merged, versus genuinely-shared loose names.
2. For the genuine ones, whether the published surface should carry a precedence signal so a consumer can resolve deterministically — e.g. a `match_type` column distinguishing preferred_term from synonym, so `Vitamin B12` → CHEBI:176843 is the documented answer.

Until (2), consumers joining on the `synonyms` column should prefer a row whose `preferred_term` equals the query.

Related: #231, #229, #218, #225.
title: 87 published labels resolve to more than one identifier, including 18 preferred_term-vs-synonym collisions

body:
Found reviewing #214.

The repo's own documented merge procedure — `.claude/skills/merge-ingredients/reference/matching-strategies.md:54-56` — is *"Mark source as REJECTED … Preserves audit trail"*, and the schema has `REJECTED: "Determined to be invalid or duplicate"` for exactly this. Two REJECTED tombstones already live in the mapped collection, so the pattern is in use.

`scripts/apply_microbedecoder_residual_merges.py` instead removes the source record outright. Synonyms and `preferred_term` are carried onto the target and `occurrence_statistics` were `0/0`, but the `notes` field is not — and that is where the upstream key lives:

    notes: Imported from microbedecoder (source_id=kgmicrobe.trait:2_dichloropropane)

Compare two records from the *same* `microbedecoder_residual_locant_fixed.tsv` batch after #211 and #214:

- `CHEBI:27789` (UNMAPPED_0722, **promoted**) → `notes: Imported from microbedecoder (source_id=kgmicrobe.trait:2_dichloroethane)`
- `CHEBI:142468` (UNMAPPED_0784, **merged**) → `notes: None`

So `kgmicrobe.trait:2_dichloropropane → CHEBI:142468` now exists nowhere in the data, while 826 other records carry their `kgmicrobe.trait` source_id. Same for `2_trichloroethane`, `1_sodium_chloride`, `1_sodium_lactate`, and the five re-routed in #214's second commit. MIM publishes to kg-microbe, so the trait id is the join key back to the source.

Related asymmetry, worth a decision rather than a fix: promoted records get an SSSOM row keyed on `preferred_term`, merged ones get none (SSSOM subjects are never synonyms — `reconcile_sssom.py:74-82`). A consumer resolving raw microbedecoder labels through the SSSOM resolves `2-dichloroethane` and silently misses `2-dichloropropane`. Defensible — the target is already mapped — but it means four rows of one manifest batch got two different treatments.

## Suggested fix

Either carry the source `notes`/source_id onto the merge target (e.g. as an additional evidence item or appended note), or tombstone as REJECTED per the documented procedure instead of deleting. Then make the merge helper and the skill doc agree, since they currently don't.
title: Merging deletes the source record instead of tombstoning it, dropping its kgmicrobe.trait source_id

From the review of PR #202.

The residual label **`sodium(+)`** (source `kgmicrobe.trait:sodium`, BacDive_Metabolite_utilization, occurrence 1) was grounded to **CHEBI:29101 `sodium(1+)`** and promoted to MAPPED (record `data/ingredients/mapped/Sodium().yaml`). The CHEBI grounding is correct for the label, but two curator questions remain:

1. **Scope:** a bare Na⁺ cation as a "utilized substrate" is closer to a phenotype/trait than a defined *media ingredient*. Consider whether this record belongs in the ingredient pipeline at all, or should be routed out like the isolation-category/phenotype residual. Occurrence is 1, so impact is negligible either way.
2. **Cosmetics:** the record file is `Sodium().yaml` with `preferred_term: Sodium(+)` (the `+` was dropped in the filename sanitiser). Curator may want to relabel the record to `sodium(1+)` and rename the file for cleanliness.

The other two applied groundings in the PR (Diacetyl → CHEBI:16583 butane-2,3-dione; Ferric Iron → CHEBI:29034 iron(3+)) are unambiguous and need no follow-up.

Note: PR #202's branch was rebuilt on the current `main` tip during review because it had been based on pre-#192 `main`; merging the stale branch would have conflicted with / reverted the merged 386-promotion + #198 work. No separate issue needed — resolved in-PR.

body:
Follow-up from the review of #199 (PR #199, `scripts/check_chebi_currency.py`).

`refresh_would_help()` decides whether re-downloading the semsql ChEBI build
would change anything by comparing the published artifact's `Content-Length`
against the local `.gz`. Equal size ⇒ same build ⇒ refresh is a no-op.

That inference is a proxy, not a proof. It cannot distinguish two builds that
happen to compress to the same length, and it reports "a refresh WOULD change
the build" for any rebuild of the *same* release whose bytes shifted.

It is deliberately the safe direction — a false "would help" costs one 760 MB
download, whereas a false "would not help" would leave someone stuck behind with
no prompt to act. And it is the strongest signal available without downloading
the artifact, which is the whole cost the check exists to avoid.

**What would actually settle it:** the semsql publisher exposes no version
endpoint we currently read. Options, roughly in order of effort:

- Range-request the first N kB of `chebi.db.gz` and read `owl:versionInfo` out of
  the decompressed prefix — gzip is streamable, so this is likely a few hundred
  kB rather than 760 MB. Needs checking that S3 honours `Range` here and that
  the `statements` row lands early enough in the file.
- Compare `ETag`/`Last-Modified` against a recorded value from the last refresh,
  which detects *change* precisely without identifying the release.

Not urgent: the current behaviour is correct in the state that actually obtains
(published == local == 252), and wrong only in the cheap direction.
title: check-chebi-currency infers 'a refresh would help' from byte size, not release

Found by the new instruction-reference check (#185).

`.claude/skills/merge-ingredients/SKILL.md` step 4 says:

> **Document flagged records** in `data/curation/flagged_duplicates.yaml` (chebi_id, record indices, reason, reviewer, resolution).

Neither `data/curation/` nor that file exists, and `git log` shows no trace of either. So an agent that merges records and dutifully "documents the flagged ones" writes to a path nothing reads, or creates a one-off directory outside every existing convention.

## Why this needs a decision rather than a path fix

The repo has since grown two surfaces that plausibly own this:

- **`history/`** (added #163) — append-only provenance, one record per session per target, scaffolded with `just new-history`. Built for exactly "which model changed what, why, under which issue".
- **`discussions:`** on the record itself — the `Discussion` supertype with `kind: CURATION_TODO` / `OPEN_QUESTION`, already carried by 8 records.

A flagged-but-unresolved duplicate is arguably a `Discussion(kind=OPEN_QUESTION)` on the surviving record, which would make it visible in the discussions browser and the knowledge-gap scan rather than sitting in a file nobody reads. But that's a curation-workflow call, not a docs fix.

## Live relevance

This isn't hypothetical: there are **61 duplicate identifier primary keys across 86 mapped records** (tracked in `NEXT_TASKS.md`), and working them will produce exactly these flags — some are clean merges, some are distinct compounds sharing an imprecise CAS, at least one is a narrowMatch judgment. Whoever picks that up needs a real place to record the "flagged, not merged" cases.

Suppressed inline with `<!-- refcheck: ignore -->` so the check stays green; remove that marker as part of the fix.
title: merge-ingredients skill directs flagged duplicates to data/curation/, which does not exist

body:
Noticed during the adversarial review of #179.

`just sync-individual` was `export-individual && validate-individual && aggregate-collections`. #179 removed `aggregate-collections` (it wrote `data/collections/`, which nothing reads) and repointed the recipe to `export-individual && validate-individual && qc-roundtrip`.

Two observations that the repoint doesn't resolve:

## 1. The gate at the end can only ever pass

`export-individual` projects `data/curated/` **over** the per-record tree, overwriting anything edited directly under `data/ingredients/`. By the time `qc-roundtrip` runs, the two surfaces necessarily agree — because the first step just made them agree by discarding one side.

So the recipe's headline ("…and verify they agree") is technically true but reads as reassurance that nothing was lost, when the verification is structurally incapable of detecting loss. The inline comment does warn that it overwrites, so this is a wording risk rather than a defect.

Also worth noting: `qc-roundtrip` runs a *second* export (into a `mktemp` copy), so the recipe exports twice. Redundant work, not a wrong write.

## 2. Nothing calls it

Grepping the repo — justfile, scripts, `.github/`, `.claude/` (skills and commands), notes, docs — turns up **no caller** for `just sync-individual`. It appears only in its own definition and in `notes/INDIVIDUAL_RECORDS.md`'s command list.

## Options

1. **Delete it.** With `sync-curated` (per-record → collection) and `qc-roundtrip` (verify) both present and used, the remaining niche is "deliberately discard per-record edits and re-project from the collection" — which is just `just export-individual`, already available and honestly named.
2. **Keep and rename**, e.g. `reproject-from-curated`, so the name states that the collection wins.

I left it alone in #179 because deleting a public recipe is a bigger call than the dead-end retirement that PR was scoped to.
title: just sync-individual has no caller and can only verify a post-destruction state

body:
Noticed during the adversarial review of #179, which retired the aggregator's and verifier's silent defaults.

#179's thesis is "no code path silently defaults to a directory". `just export-individual` (justfile) still runs:

```
uv run python scripts/export_individual_records.py
```

with no `--input-dir` / `--output-dir`, relying on the script's defaults.

**This is not a bug today** — those defaults are `data/curated/` and `data/ingredients/`, which are the correct directories, and the recipe is the intended way to project the collection onto the per-record tree. So unlike `aggregate_records.py`, the default doesn't point somewhere nothing reads.

It's filed for consistency, not urgency: it's the same *shape* as the pattern #169 retired, and the reason that pattern was dangerous is that a default which is silently wrong is indistinguishable from one that is silently right until something moves.

## Options

1. **Leave it.** Defensible — the defaults are correct and the recipe is a convenience wrapper. If so, worth a one-line comment in the script saying the defaults are load-bearing so nobody "tidies" them.
2. **Pass them explicitly in the recipe**, matching `qc-roundtrip` and `sync-curated`, which both now spell out their directories. Costs two lines, removes the asymmetry.

Low priority either way.
title: just export-individual relies on implicit default directories
